start.heading: Start the activity
start.storyEyebrow: Coffee supply-chain simulation · From farm to shelf
start.storyIntro: You will take on the work of each party in the supply chain in turn -- producer, certifying body, carrier, processing plant, and regulator. Along the way you will follow one batch of coffee and see how each transaction is recorded on the ledger.
start.heroAlt: The journey of a coffee batch from a Lâm Đồng highland farm, through transport and roasting, to a retail shelf.
start.heroCaption: A batch of coffee passes through many handovers. Every transaction leaves a trace on the ledger that can be checked.
start.objectivesHeading: After completing this activity, you will be able to:
start.objective1: Explain how a physical batch is represented as a digital asset on the ledger.
start.objective3: Distinguish an asset's current state from its related transaction history.
start.objective4: Explain why an error is handled by appending a correcting transaction rather than deleting the original record.
start.objective5: Determine recall scope from the provenance relationships between batches.
start.objective6: Explain the limits of blockchain in guaranteeing the truthfulness of input data.
start.scoringPass: A total of {points} points or more.
start.scoringHint: A hint only affects the score for the activity it directly supports. Before you open one, you will see which activity is affected and the most it can cost.
start.scoringRetry: Each activity is scored by how many attempts it takes. Getting it right first time earns the highest credit; later attempts are worth less at most. Even so, completing a required business action always earns at least {percent}% of its points.
start.restartConfirmBody: All progress and scores from your previous session will be deleted. This cannot be undone.

stage.orientation.title: Step 1 – Meet the simulated blockchain network
stage.orientation.instruction: Before writing anything to the ledger, look at the real supply chain and the organizations in it. The coffee batch is a physical object; the ledger record is only a digital representation of it.
stage.orientation.supplyChainAlt: Supply chain diagram: producer co-operative, certification body, logistics provider, processing plant, distributor, retailer, consumer and regulator.
stage.orientation.journeyCaption: Follow the coffee batch through production, transport, processing, and retail; each handoff adds evidence.
stage.orientation.checkQuestion: Does blockchain automatically prove that the original data is true?
stage.orientation.checkOptionYes: Yes. Once data is on a blockchain it is certainly true.
stage.orientation.checkOptionNo: No. Blockchain helps establish who wrote the data and whether it has changed, but it does not prove the data is true.
stage.orientation.checkOptionPartly: Yes, if the transaction is endorsed by several organizations.
stage.orientation.checkFeedback: Blockchain can help establish who recorded data, when it was recorded, and whether it has been altered; but the truthfulness of the input still has to be verified by procedures, inspections, and the accountability of the participating organizations.
stage.orientation.noPenaltyNotice: This question is not scored. It is here so you can check your own starting assumptions.
stage.createBatch.title: Step 2 – Create the coffee batch on the ledger
stage.createBatch.instruction: You are the production manager at the co-operative. Create the record for the green coffee batch just harvested. This is the batch's first transaction, and it will be written into the first block of the ledger.
stage.createBatch.action.create: Create the record for the green coffee batch weighing 100 kg and write the transaction into the first block.
stage.createBatch.sealBlock: Write the transaction into a block
stage.createBatch.sealBlockHelp: In a real blockchain a block may contain many transactions. Here we write it immediately so you can watch the first block form.
stage.anchorCertificate.title: Step 3 – Anchor the quality certificate
stage.shipAndMonitor.title: Step 4 – Hand over and monitor transport
stage.receiveAndCorrect.title: Step 5 – Receive the batch and correct the error
stage.transformBatch.title: Step 6 – Transform green coffee into roasted coffee
stage.packageAndDistribute.title: Step 7 – Package and distribute the finished product
stage.verifyAndTamper.title: Step 8 – Verify provenance and attempt tampering
stage.recallAndDebrief.title: Step 9 – Trace and recall the product
stage.anchorCertificate.instruction: You are the certification officer. Assess the certificate, its issuer, its storage, and whether the lot may continue before recording any evidence.
stage.shipAndMonitor.instruction: The co-operative hands the batch to the carrier. Decide what this transaction actually transfers, then record the transport conditions the sensor reports.
stage.receiveAndCorrect.instruction: The plant receives and reweighs the batch. The committed manifest declares 1000 kg while the measured quantity is 100 kg. The original record remains unchanged; append a correction so the effective declared quantity becomes 100 kg.
stage.receiveAndCorrect.action.receive: Receive the batch from the carrier and record the purchase of ownership.
stage.receiveAndCorrect.action.correct: Append a correction of the manifest's declaredQuantity from 1000 kg to 100 kg; the original record is not edited.
stage.transformBatch.instruction: Roast 100 kg of green coffee into 82 kg of roasted coffee. The input batch is marked as consumed, and a provenance relationship is created between the two.
stage.transformBatch.action.transform: Roast 100 kg of green coffee into 82 kg of roasted coffee and record the provenance link.
stage.packageAndDistribute.instruction: Package 82 kg of roasted coffee into 820 packages of 100 g, transfer ownership to the distributor while the goods remain at the plant, then ship to the retailer.
stage.packageAndDistribute.action.packag: Package 82 kg of roasted coffee into 820 units of 100 g.
stage.packageAndDistribute.action.dispat: Transfer ownership to the distributor, then dispatch the goods to the retailer.
stage.verifyAndTamper.instruction: View the public information a consumer sees when scanning the QR code, then try altering an old record on a copy of the ledger and observe what happens.
stage.verifyAndTamper.workspace.title: Blockchain verification laboratory
stage.verifyAndTamper.workspace.descript: Inspect committed records, compare role-visible provenance, and run controlled integrity checks on copies.
stage.verifyAndTamper.workspace.inspecto: Select a block and transaction to inspect their SHA-256 digests and recorded chain link.
stage.verifyAndTamper.publicHeading: Public information shown when the QR code is scanned
stage.verifyAndTamper.publicNotice: This is what a consumer sees. Wholesale prices and internal data do not appear here, although they remain on the ledger where only authorised parties can read them.
stage.verifyAndTamper.tamperHeading: Try altering a record that has already been committed
stage.verifyAndTamper.tamperIntro: The simulation copies the ledger, then alters the quantity on one transaction in the copy. Your real ledger is not affected.
stage.verifyAndTamper.step1Detail: Transaction {transaction} was changed from {original} to {tampered}. The record no longer matches its own hash, so the system detects it immediately.
stage.verifyAndTamper.step2Detail: If the forger recomputes the hash to match, the transaction stops being flagged. But the block containing it committed to the old hash, so block {block} no longer matches.
stage.verifyAndTamper.step3Detail: Repairing the block hash makes block {block} match again, but the next block recorded the old hash, so that link breaks. Hiding this one means repairing the next block, and the one after it, all the way to the end of the chain.
stage.verifyAndTamper.conclusion: None of those steps was prevented. In this simulation, the change makes the hash chain inconsistent, so an integrity check can detect its trace. Repairing one layer only exposes the next.
stage.verifyAndTamper.hashesAreReal: The hashing in this simulation is real: SHA-256, computed from the contents of the records themselves. The broken hash chain you just saw is therefore a genuine computed result, not a staged animation. The signatures and the organization identities are still simulated.
stage.verifyAndTamper.hashesAndSignature: The hashing and digital signatures in this simulation use genuine cryptographic operations: SHA-256 and Ed25519. Organizational identities, educational keys, the network, and the ordering service remain learning simulations.
stage.verifyAndTamper.signatureDemoHeadi: Check what happens when signed content changes
stage.verifyAndTamper.signatureDemoIntro: Open this optional demonstration to verify a signed proposal, change one character in a copy, recompute its digest, and verify it again with the original signature. Your transaction and ledger are not changed.
stage.verifyAndTamper.modifiedSignatureR: Modified copy: the original signature no longer matches
stage.verifyAndTamper.signatureDemoConcl: The signature is bound to the proposal's exact content. Changing that content changes the proposal digest, so the original signature no longer verifies.
stage.verifyAndTamper.signatureDemoFaile: The signature check could not run on this copy.
stage.verifyAndTamper.ledgerIntact: Your real ledger is intact: the demonstration ran only on a copy.
stage.recallAndDebrief.instruction: A laboratory finds an unacceptable pesticide residue in the original green coffee batch. Trace forward to identify exactly the affected lots, and only those.
stage.recallAndDebrief.commandCenterDesc: Reconcile the laboratory finding with provenance, location, and custody before setting the scope and handing the order to the proper authority.
stage.recallAndDebrief.consumerRiskHigh: High — finished goods are at retail
stage.recallAndDebrief.affectedDescendan: Descendant lots with a provenance path
stage.recallAndDebrief.sceneAlt: A laboratory worker tests a coffee sample while a food-safety inspector and supermarket manager compare lots and isolate one group of products for recall.
stage.recallAndDebrief.scopeNotice: Use the provenance recorded on the ledger, not the product name. One lot closely resembles the contaminated one: same co-operative, harvested a day later, roasted the same day at the same plant.
stage.recallAndDebrief.recallPending: Answer the scope question above first. The recall is filed for exactly the lots you selected.
stage.recallAndDebrief.unauthorizedFeedb: Your scope and evidence were recorded, but this role is not authorized to commit a recall. No ledger state or asset version changed.
stage.recallAndDebrief.precommitHandoffP: Before submitting, decide whether the active organization should keep responsibility or use one of the scenario-permitted handoffs. Authorization is evaluated from the resulting trusted context, not from learner-entered identity.
stage.recallAndDebrief.handoffPrompt: The initial decision is locked. Use a scenario-permitted organizational handoff to continue.
stage.recallAndDebrief.handoffComplete: The trusted organizational handoff is complete. Review the scope, then submit the recall under the active context.
stage.recallAndDebrief.resubmitAuthorize: Resubmit the recall under authorized authority
stage.recallAndDebrief.reasonAffected: Included because the ledger records this provenance path from the contaminated batch:
stage.recallAndDebrief.reasonUnaffected: No provenance path leads here from the contaminated batch, however similar the label looks. Recalling it destroys good stock.
stage.recallAndDebrief.missedHeading: Affected lots you did not select
stage.recallAndDebrief.missedNote: These stay on sale. Leaving contaminated product on a shelf is the costlier of the two mistakes, which is why it is scored more heavily.
stage.recallAndDebrief.accuracyExact: The recall scope is exact: every affected lot and no others.
stage.recallAndDebrief.accuracyMissed: {count} affected lot(s) missed. Contaminated product is still on the shelf.

report.causalHeading: How earlier decisions affected the outcome
report.causal.certificateStrong: At Stage 3, you verified the certificate and issuer and retained the document off chain with an on-chain hash. At Stage 9, that evidence could be used without additional review.
report.causal.certificateReviewed: At Stage 3, the initial certificate assessment required issuer review. At Stage 9, {count} record(s) therefore required manual review before the evidence could be relied on.
report.causal.certificateWeak: At Stage 3, certificate or issuer concerns were left unresolved. At Stage 9, the certificate remained weak recall evidence.
report.causal.storageRemediated: At Stage 3, the initial storage choice was remediated by retaining the document off chain and its hash on chain. The correction preserved confidentiality but added operational work.
report.causal.storageExposure: At Stage 3, the full document was selected for on-chain storage. That weakens data governance and creates an avoidable confidentiality risk.
report.causal.signatureInvalidRejected: A proposal carried a signature that no longer matched its signed content. That submission remained only in audit history and created no ledger transaction.
report.causal.signatureUnknownRejected: At Stage 3, the cryptographic check found a valid signature but the organizational identity was not recognized. The submission was rejected and did not enter the ledger.

check.certificateStorage.question: The quality certificate is a PDF of about 2 MB. How should it be recorded on the ledger?
check.certificateStorage.optionWholeFile: Store the entire PDF file on chain.
check.certificateStorage.optionHash: Store the file off chain, and record its hash and metadata on chain.
check.certificateStorage.optionFilename: Record only the filename on chain.
check.certificateStorage.feedback: Off chain with an on-chain hash is the right choice. A large file need not sit on the chain; the hash is enough to detect whether it changed. Recording only a filename lets the file behind that name be swapped without the ledger noticing.
check.certificateStorage.connection: You have just anchored the certificate's hash. The hash tells you whether the file changed; it does not tell you whether what the file says is true.
check.certificateIssuer.question: How should the certificate issuer be classified for this case?
check.certificateIssuer.optionRecognized: The issuer is recognized and authorized to certify product quality.
The issuer is recognized, but is not authorized for quality certification.
check.certificateIssuer.optionUnrecogniz: The issuer is not recognized by this permissioned network.
check.certificateIssuer.optionAcceptHash: Accept it: a valid hash proves the document has not been altered.
check.certificateIssuer.optionReject: Reject it: the issuer has no certification authority on this network.
check.certificateIssuer.optionAcceptNote: Accept it, but note that it is unverified.
check.certificateIssuer.feedback: Identity, recognition and authorization are separate checks. A valid hash does not grant an issuer authority.
check.certificateIssuer.connection: Compare the issuer with the permissioned network's organization registry and authorization rules.
check.custodyScope.question: The co-operative hands the batch to the carrier for transport to the plant. What does this transaction transfer?
check.custodyScope.feedback: Custody only. The carrier holds and transports the batch, but does not buy it. Ownership stays with the co-operative until a separate sale takes place.
check.custodyScope.connection: Choosing both makes RULE_OWNERSHIP_UNCHANGED_ON_CUSTODY_TRANSFER reject the transaction. This is the most important distinction in the whole activity.
check.transportCondition.question: The sensor reports 72% humidity against a 70% limit. How should this be recorded?
check.transportCondition.optionIgnore: Ignore it: the difference is small.
check.transportCondition.optionInspect: Record the excursion, flag the batch for inspection, keep the raw dataset off chain and anchor its hash.
check.transportCondition.optionWholeFile: Store the whole sensor dataset on chain.
check.transportCondition.feedback: Record it and flag for inspection. An excursion does not by itself condemn a batch; it creates an obligation to look. The blockchain records the reading, a person decides what it means.
check.transportCondition.connection: Sensor data reaches the ledger through an authorized data source. A blockchain cannot measure humidity by itself.
check.transformationProvenance.question: After roasting, how is the roasted batch recorded relative to the green coffee it came from?
check.transformationProvenance.optionInd: As an entirely new batch, unrelated to the input.
check.transformationProvenance.optionLin: As a new batch with a provenance link to the input, which is marked as consumed.
check.transformationProvenance.optionDel: The input batch is deleted from the ledger.
check.transformationProvenance.feedback: The new batch keeps a link to its input, and the input is marked as consumed rather than deleted. That link is exactly what makes forward tracing from green coffee to a finished package possible.
check.transformationProvenance.connectio: Without that link, at the recall stage you would have no way to know which packages came from the contaminated batch.
check.tamperIntegrity.question: You just altered an old record on a copy of the ledger and saw that block and every block after it report an error. What does that prove?
check.tamperIntegrity.optionPrevents: Blockchain prevents anyone from altering old data.
check.tamperIntegrity.optionDetectable: Blockchain does not prevent alteration; it creates hash-chain inconsistencies that an integrity check can detect.
check.tamperIntegrity.optionLastBlock: Only the last block is affected.
check.tamperIntegrity.feedback: Blockchain produces evidence of tampering; it does not prevent tampering. Because each block carries the previous block's hash, altering an old record invalidates every block that follows.
check.tamperIntegrity.connection: That demonstration ran on a copy. Your real ledger was not touched.
check.dataGovernance.question: Classify each of these data items according to how it should be handled in this scenario.
check.dataGovernance.categoryOffChainHas: Store off chain and anchor the hash
check.dataGovernance.categoryDoNotCollec: Should not be collected for this purpose
check.dataGovernance.feedback: The right classification depends on the situation, not on a universal rule. Here: batch identifier and recall status are needed by everyone, so they go on chain; large files stay off chain with only a hash anchored; wholesale price is commercially sensitive; a consumer's home address is not needed for traceability at all and should not be collected.

check.recallScope.question: The laboratory found an unacceptable residue in green coffee batch BAT_GREEN_COFFEE_001. Which lots fall within the recall?
check.recallScope.optionNearMissLot: Packaged lot BAT_PACKAGED_COFFEE_002 (Arabica Lam Dong 100g, roasted the same day at the same plant)
check.challengeRecall.question: The incident identifies a source asset in this case. Use the provenance paths to select every listed asset within its recall scope.
check.challengeRecall.optionPrimary: The packaged lot created in this case
check.challengeRecall.optionAncestor: The roasted batch in the case lineage
check.challengeRecall.optionSource: The original green-coffee batch in the case lineage
check.challengeRecall.optionNearMiss: A similar packaged lot with a separate provenance path
check.recallScope.feedback: The recall covers the roasted batch and the packaged lot derived from the contaminated green coffee. BAT_PACKAGED_COFFEE_002 looks almost identical: same variety, same region, same plant, roasted the same day. But it came from a different green batch and has no provenance path to the contaminated one. Only provenance separates them.
check.recallScope.connection: Recalling too widely destroys good stock; recalling too narrowly leaves contaminated product on the shelf. Both are errors, with different consequences.
check.blockchainNecessity.question: When is blockchain more clearly warranted than a centralized database?
check.blockchainNecessity.optionAlwaysBe: Always: blockchain is more secure than a database.
check.blockchainNecessity.optionIndepend: When independent organizations need shared records but do not want one participant controlling the whole system.
check.blockchainNecessity.optionFaster: When higher throughput than a database is needed.
check.blockchainNecessity.optionGuarante: When a guarantee that the input data is true is needed.
check.blockchainNecessity.feedback: Blockchain is most defensible when independent organizations need shared records and none should control the whole system. If a single organization owns the data, a database is usually simpler, faster and cheaper. And no system can guarantee that the input data is true.

terms.transactionDefinition: A record of a supply-chain event, submitted to the network for validation and writing into the ledger.
terms.blockDefinition: A group of transactions written together, containing the hash of the previous block.
terms.hashDefinition: A string computed from data content. If the data changes, the hash changes, so it can be used to detect alteration.
terms.ledgerDefinition: The whole chain of blocks and the transactions recorded in them.
terms.worldStateDefinition: The current state of each asset, derived from the whole transaction history.
terms.smartContractDefinition: A program running on the blockchain network that checks and enforces business rules. In this simulation, the rule engine plays that role.
terms.ownershipDefinition: The right of ownership over goods. The owner may sell the batch.
terms.custodyDefinition: Physical possession of goods. The custodian is holding them but does not necessarily own them.
terms.provenanceDefinition: The relationships between lots, showing which was derived from which.
terms.endorsementDefinition: Approval of a transaction by the organizations concerned, before it is recorded.
terms.orderingServiceDefinition: The component that puts transactions in order before they are written into a block.
terms.oracleDefinition: An authorized external data source that brings real-world information onto the ledger, such as a sensor reading.
terms.permissionedBlockchainDefinition: A blockchain network on which only recognized organizations may write transactions.

counterfactual.isolated: Only the selected decision changed; compatible later decisions were replayed.
counterfactual.compound: The selected decision changed and the branch requires or contains later decisions. Not every difference can be attributed to the first change.
counterfactual.noStateDifference: No final role-visible business or ledger-state difference was observed.
counterfactual.attribution.DIRECT_INTERV: The case rule links this change directly to the alternative decision.

counterfactual.attribution.LATER_DECISIO: Later choices also changed, so this difference cannot be attributed only to the first alternative.
counterfactual.attribution.STOCHASTIC_OU: This difference came from a named stochastic outcome.
counterfactual.attribution.CONDITION_OVE: This difference came from the explicitly changed scenario condition.

counterfactual.noneRevealedLater: No additional role-visible evidence record was released after this decision.
counterfactual.gradePreserved: The original score, completion status, ratings, and competency evidence remain unchanged. The alternative is ungraded.
counterfactual.continuationRequired: This is a compound branch. A later decision must be completed before reflection can be submitted.
counterfactual.reflection.reasonForDiffe: Why did the alternative produce a different result?
